summary: Outlines one potential approach for inter-domain routing in future global internets. It is an informational paper put forward for discussion, not a protocol standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A proposal for how the big networks of the world could tell each other the best way to send mail between them, shared as an idea to talk about.

subtitle: A proposal to combine hop-by-hop path-vector routing with on-demand source routing for large internets.

tldr.problem: Inter-domain routing has to scale to very large networks and still support special routes with policy and type-of-service needs, and the two main approaches each handle only one of those well.
tldr.mechanism: Node routing (NR) uses path-vector, hop-by-hop routing with aggregation for common routes. Source-demand routing (SDR) lets a source domain compute and install special routes on demand using link-state information.
tldr.outcome: The memo is informational and outlines one potential approach. It does not specify a standard, and it states that the architecture is a goal for the next 5 years, not a short-term deployment.

today: RFC 1322 is an Informational memo that does not specify a standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It outlines one potential approach, and the text does not say that the architecture was adopted.

sections.title: The Inter-Domain Routing Problem
sections.content:
The global internet is split into domains, each under one administration. Routing within a domain is intra-domain (interior) routing, and routing across domains is inter-domain (exterior) routing. Border routers (BRs) forward packets across domain boundaries, and route servers (RSs) exchange inter-domain routing information.

The number and variety of routing needs is growing because of transit restrictions, different types of service and multiple carriers with different charging schemes. The memo says current work has split into two camps. One is represented by BGP and IDRP, the other by Inter-Domain Policy Routing (IDPR). The authors argue that the two are complementary and not mutually exclusive.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet is made of many separate networks run by different owners. They need a way to agree on routes between them, and there are two ideas that people have argued about.

sections.title: Two Components: NR and SDR
sections.content:
The architecture has two parts. Node routing (NR) computes and installs routes shared by many sources. These generic routes warrant wide propagation, so aggregation matters. Source-demand routing (SDR) computes and installs specialized routes that too few sources share to justify NR. Routes needed only sporadically are also candidates for SDR.

The memo uses a manufacturing analogy: NR is the off-the-shelf route and SDR is the special order. The SDR information exchange relies on services from NR, so every domain is required to implement and take part in NR. The memo adds that supporting highly specialized routes for all source-destination pairs is not feasible in any foreseeable architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: NR is the ready-made route everyone shares. SDR is the custom route made only when someone asks for it.

sections.title: Requirements and Priorities
sections.content:
Complexity is judged by storage, computation and message overhead. Storage in the routing and forwarding information bases should grow significantly slower than linearly (close to logarithmically) with the number of domains. Computation must never become exponential. Bandwidth matters less, especially with incremental updates.

Aggregation is treated as essential, done by forming confederations of domains. They must be formed without global coordination, may overlap without being nested, and different domains may aggregate differently. The architecture must support transit policies and heterogeneous route selection policies, and lets domains hide routing information on a need-to-know basis. Several policies are explicitly not supported, such as route selection or transit policies that depend on external behavior, and load-sensitive routing for generic routes.
sections.plainLanguage: A good plan must not need a giant notebook as the internet grows. Groups of networks should be able to team up, and each owner keeps its own rules.

sections.title: Node Routing Uses Path Vector
sections.content:
The memo compares link state (LS) and path vector (PV) for NR. In path vector, each border router advertises reachable destinations together with path attributes, including the sequence of domains the route has passed through. That path attribute is used to suppress loops. BGP and IDRP are examples, and the memo considers only IDRP because BGP is a proper subset of it in functionality.

The authors argue that PV scales better. Each domain picks routes using only local policy, so heterogeneous selection policies add little cost. PV allows confederations to be nested, disjoint or overlapping, restricts distribution of policy information, and supports selective information hiding. They state that they know of no sub-exponential LS algorithm for heterogeneous route selection policies. They therefore choose PV for NR.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network passes along a route together with the list of networks it passed through, so loops are easy to spot, and each network can pick its favourite route.

sections.title: Source-Demand Routing
sections.content:
In SDR the domain that originates the traffic computes and installs the route. This is link-state style, using an IDPR-like design in which updates carry explicit policy terms. SDR does not need a complete global map, and the memo assumes the number of SDR routes installed in a border router should be on the order of log N, where N is the number of routing domains.

Forwarding uses two techniques: loose source routing, which names a sequence of domains with no per-connection state, and route setup, in which setup packets install a path ID at each border router and an accept message returns hop by hop. A source can allow fallback to an NR route if setup fails or the route later fails, as long as policy allows. Open questions include how to distribute configured information without global flooding and how to share dynamic status, for which the memo proposes small hop-count flooding plus reverse path update (RPU).
sections.plainLanguage: For a special trip, the sender plans the whole path and tells each stop along the way. If the special path breaks, it may be allowed to use the shared route instead.

sections.title: Unification and Transition
sections.content:
The memo lists areas for more commonality between NR and SDR: a shared routing information base, NR path vectors that point to repositories for SDR information, a standard network header such as IP or CLNP with option fields, and unified reachability information. The architecture is meant to accommodate IP, CLNP and ST-II, and does not decide whether one protocol or several will serve different network layers.

It is not intended for full deployment in the short term. It is proposed as a goal for the next 5 years. The NR component may be phased in gradually, for example by replacing existing EGP-2 routing with BGP for IP, and SDR can be added afterwards. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody has to change everything at once. Networks can adopt the shared routes first and add the special-order feature later.
